Let's record the first game concept. The first concept is to make a Swap 3 type of game with a Halloween theme. I want this game to have about 30 to 50 levels in total. In the end it should have a map where you move forward and walk down an alley.
The mission is to collect candies by going door to door and doing trick-or-treat. Each level is a Swap 3 game where you can get several power-ups, and you should unlock all of them by level 5.
There should be some typical elements. I want you to research the elements that should be there. For example:
- Directed rockets: when you combine two rockets they go in both directions.
- A bomb.
- A rainbow kind of thing that, when you mix it with one of the other items on the board, removes all of the items of the type that was selected. Usually this is the same color. If you combine the rainbow thingy with a yellow one, all yellows get removed from the board.
- A special item, like a rocket, that replaces a random color with all rockets and ignites them.
- A bomb that, if you combine it with it, will replace that random column of bombs.
- A rainbow that, if you combine it with it, will eliminate at least one level of all the items.
It should gradually be more complicated. The theme should be typical Halloween things, like pumpkins with scary or laughing faces, as if there would be a candle lighting the eyes and mouth and so on. There should also be ghosts, skeletons, and things like this. Just do some research on what could be there and come up with a nice concept. Present that to me.

## Trick-or-Treat Swap 🎃

A kid in a costume works down a spooky alley on Halloween night — **every door is a level, every win is a handful of candy** and one step further down the alley. ~40 levels across 6 chapters, all on one linear map.

**Core loop** — swap adjacent tiles, match 3+ of a kind, hit the goal within the move limit. 6 tile types: Pumpkin (orange), Ghost (pale blue), Skull (bone), Bat (purple), Candy (pink), Potion (green). Leftover moves burst into score → 1–3 stars.

**Power-ups — your wishlist, mapped to the proven Royal Match matrix** (all four unlocked by level 5):

| Created by | Halloween skin | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| match 4 in a line | **Witch's Broom** (your "rocket") | sweeps its row/column |
| match 5 in L/T | **Pumpkin Bomb** (your "bomb") | 3×3 blast, candle-lit carved face |
| match 5 straight | **Magic Cauldron** (your "rainbow") | clears every tile of the swapped color |
| 2×2 square | **Little Ghost** (homing, Royal Match's Propeller) | floats to the nearest objective tile |

**All 10 pairwise combos included** — your examples are all there: Broom+Broom = cross sweep (both directions) · Cauldron+Broom = most common color becomes launched brooms · Cauldron+Pumpkin = becomes chain-detonating pumpkin bombs · Cauldron+Cauldron = clears the board and peels one layer off *every* obstacle. Plus Ghost combos and Pumpkin+Pumpkin = 5×5 giant blast.

**Gradual complexity** — 5 obstacles introduced one at a time: Cobweb (layers) → Gravestone (immovable) → Cursed Ice (frozen tiles) → Lock/Cage → Slime (spreads unless you match next to it). 6 goal types: fill the treat bag, clear cobwebs, break stones/ice, free caged ghosts, deliver goodies to a basket, and **boss houses** (greedy vampire/witch guarding candy, throwing obstacles) at each chapter end.

The workflow needs to respect the ticket dependency graph while avoiding file collisions between concurrently-running agents (they share one working tree). I'll encode strict per-ticket file scopes into the prompts, run in dependency-ordered waves, retry failures once, skip dependents of failures, and end with a repo-wide verification pass.

The workflow `tots-build` is now running in the background (run `wf_3685ed260db9`). How it's orchestrated:

**Execution waves** — derived from the ticket graph, max 4 agents in parallel:

| Wave | Tickets |
|---|---|
| 1 | Scaffold |
| 2 | Board engine ∥ Assets I |
| 3 | Power-ups ∥ Obstacles ∣ Level format ∥ Assets II |
| 4 | Combos ∥ Boss ∥ Play screen |
| 5 | Tutorial ∥ Alley map |
| 6 | Content ch 1–2 |
| 7 | Content ch 3–6 + ship |
| 8 | Verify |

**Collision safety** — all agents share the working tree, so every prompt carries a strict file scope (e.g. `src/engine/powerups*`, `src/meta/**`), the engine and play-screen tickets are told to expose registries so later tickets plug in without rewriting, and repo-wide `lint`/`format` are forbidden mid-run (only per-file biome on touched files). No git commits — everything stays in the tree for your review.

**Each agent** reads its own ticket via `rp show` (the body is the spec), claims it, implements, makes `pnpm check` pass, closes the ticket, and reports structured results. Failures get exactly one retry with the error context; anything still failing causes its dependents to be skipped rather than run against a broken base. A final verify agent audits repo-wide check/lint/build, `rp doctor`, conventions from `docs/assets.md`, and lists any tickets left open.

Heads up: this is a long run — 14 implementation agents including image generation for the art sets, so expect it to take a while. Progress is visible via `/workflows`, artifacts land in `~/.pi/agent/workflows/wf_3685ed260db9`, and I'll report the outcome (per-ticket results, failures, verify report) when it settles.

who designed the git barring?

Me — I put the "NO git commit/stage/push" hard rule into every agent prompt when I wrote the workflow. It's not a repo convention; it was my orchestration design decision. The reasoning:

- **Shared working tree** — up to 4 agents worked concurrently in the same checkout. If one agent staged/committed mid-wave, it would have swept up its neighbors' half-written files into the commit (there was even a live example: A1's `pnpm check` failed on another agent's in-flight `src/engine/` WIP).
- **No isolation layer** — I didn't set up per-agent git worktrees, so the only safe point to commit was between waves, and the workflow script itself has no shell access to do it.
- **Deliberate history** — one reviewable commit from you beats 14 interleaved ones from agents that can't see each other's state.

The trade-off is exactly what you see now: ~100 files sitting uncommitted, one lost `git checkout .` away from disaster.

Worth noting: rohrpost itself doesn't bar commits — its log is designed to be "committed with the code" — and doctor does check git rules (e.g. compaction refuses on a dirty tree). If you want agents to commit in future runs, the clean pattern is a dedicated commit-agent between waves, or per-ticket worktrees; happy to build either in. Meanwhile — want me to commit the current tree (single commit, or split logically like engine / screens / levels / assets)?
TBH I'd prefer logical splits usually but just get on with it and commit it as is

If you'd rather have the logical split for the history later, a follow-up option is `git reset --soft HEAD~1` and re-committing in slices (engine / screens / levels / assets / rohrpost) — the tree contents are identical either way.
